notes.meaning: Kohath was the second son of Levi, and his four sons formed the four Kohathite clans. Moses and Aaron belonged to the Amramite clan, which gave this family a place of special honor. Even so, Moses sought no special titles or privileges for his own sons, who remained ordinary Levites.

All Kohathite males who were at least one month old were counted, making a total of 8,600. Even though baby boys could not work yet, they were set apart from infancy to be trained for holy duties. When grown, they were responsible for caring for the most sacred objects of the sanctuary, God's holy tent.

The Kohathite families were instructed to camp on the south side of the tabernacle. In the layout of the camp, this was a place of high rank, second only to the eastern entrance. This position placed them right next to the tribe of Reuben.

Elizaphan was appointed leader over all the Kohathite clans. He came from the family of Uzziel, who was Kohath's youngest son. God often chooses leaders according to His own purposes rather than by age or birth order.

The Kohathites were given charge of the holiest items inside the tabernacle. These included the ark of the covenant, the table for holy bread, the golden lampstand, the altars, and the inner curtain. These sacred furnishings had to be covered by the priests before the Kohathites could carry them on their shoulders.

Eleazar, the eldest surviving son of Aaron the high priest, was placed in charge over all the Levite leaders. He supervised the whole tribe and had direct oversight of the Kohathites who carried the most holy objects. He was being prepared to step into his father's place as high priest in the years ahead.
Merari was Levi's third son, and from him came two clans named after his sons Mahli and Mushi. These two families formed the third major division of the tribe of Levi.
The Merarite males aged one month and older totaled 6,200. This made them the smallest of the three Levite branches.
Zuriel was named the chief over the Merarite families. Their assigned camp was on the north side of the tabernacle, between the sacred tent and the camp of Dan.

The Merarites were given charge of the heavy building frame of the tabernacle and its surrounding courtyard. Their duty was to pack, carry, and set up the wooden wall frames, crossbars, posts, metal bases, tent pegs, and ropes. Because these materials were so heavy, God later provided them with ox carts to help move the load.

Moses, Aaron, and the priests camped on the east side directly facing the sunrise in front of the tabernacle entrance. This was the place of highest honor because it guarded the only way into God's dwelling. Anyone unauthorized who tried to enter or do priestly work was to be put to death, protecting the holiness of God.

The total count of Levite males a month old or older was 22,000. God claimed this entire tribe as His own special portion to serve Him in the wilderness. Levi was by far the smallest tribe in Israel, reminding God's people that He often accomplishes His greatest work through a smaller flock.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars note that adding the three clan totals (7,500, 8,600, and 6,200) yields 22,300, and suggest a scribe miscopied the Hebrew letter for 3 as 6 in verse 28.

notes.meaning: God told Moses to take a separate count of every firstborn male in the other twelve tribes who was at least one month old. Each name was recorded on an official list. This careful count prepared the way for God's plan to exchange the Levites for Israel's firstborn sons.

God declared that the Levites would belong to Him instead of the firstborn sons of Israel. In the same way, the animals of the Levites would stand in for the firstborn livestock of the other tribes. God repeated "I am the LORD" to remind them that He has the right to claim His people and set them apart for His work.
Moses obeyed the Lord and counted all the firstborn sons throughout the nation of Israel. He carried out God's command exactly and without hesitation.

The count showed that Israel had 22,273 firstborn males who were a month old or older. This meant there were 273 more firstborn sons in Israel than there were Levite males. The close match between the numbers shows how God plans all things with exact care.

The Lord repeated His order to take the Levites and their livestock as substitutes for Israel's firstborn. Repeating the command showed how important this holy exchange was to God. From that day on, the Levites belonged directly to the Lord for His worship and service.

Because there were 273 more firstborn Israelites than Levites, a ransom price had to be paid for the extra boys. To redeem someone means to pay a price to buy them back and free them from an obligation. God set the price at five silver coins, called shekels, based on the official weight kept at the sanctuary.

God told Moses to give the redemption money directly to Aaron and his sons. Because the priests received 273 fewer Levite helpers than there were firstborn sons, the silver was given to them as fair compensation. This money helped maintain the worship of the sanctuary.

Moses collected the silver ransom for every firstborn son who was not matched by a Levite. The 22,000 Levites had redeemed 22,000 firstborn sons, leaving exactly 273 to be redeemed by money. Every single person was accounted for with complete fairness.

Moses collected 1,365 silver shekels from the families of the firstborn. This matched the math precisely, paying five shekels for each of the 273 extra sons. The payment was measured by the sanctuary standard to ensure that every coin was full weight.

Moses gave all the silver to Aaron and the priests, just as the Lord had commanded. Moses proved to be an honest and faithful manager of God's house, keeping nothing for himself. This payment points ahead to Jesus Christ, who paid the ultimate price to redeem us from sin.
